title: The Desert Childhood
subtitle: The Prophet's Early Years with Halimah al-Sa'diyyah
summary: The Arabian custom of desert wet-nursing, Halimah al-Sa'diyyah taking the infant Muhammad ﷺ to the desert territories of Banu Sa'd, the blessing in her household, his mastery of pure Arabic, and the childhood cleansing in the pasture.

sections.text: The Aristocratic Custom of Desert Fostering

In the urban settlements of pre-Islamic Arabia, particularly within the patrician merchant clans of Quraysh, it was customary for families to place their newborn infants with bedouin foster mothers in the open desert. Known as the tradition of istirda' (wet-nursing and desert fosterage), this practice served vital physical, linguistic, and cultural purposes in shaping future leaders.

Biographers explain that the confined stone valley of Makkah, hemmed in by bare mountains, was hot and prone to illness, whereas the open desert offered clean air and a hardier upbringing for children.
The expansive sands and rolling gravel plateaus of the Arabian desert highlands.
The Linguistic Sanctuary of Banu Sa'd

Equally paramount was the preservation of speech. Makkah, as an international transit hub frequented by merchants from Yemen, Syria, Abyssinia, and Persia, experienced an inevitable dilution of its native tongue. In the isolated encampments of the desert tribes, however, the Arabic language retained its purest morphology, uncorrupted phonology, and rich metaphorical vocabulary.

Among all the nomadic tribes of the peninsula, none enjoyed a higher reputation for linguistic eloquence, graceful dialect, and moral integrity than the Hawazin tribe of Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr, whose pastures lay in the rugged mountainous country south-east of Ta'if. It was from this tribe that wet-nurses journeyed biannually to Makkah in search of foster infants.
A Year of Drought and the Arrival of Halimah

The account that follows comes from the report attributed to Halimah herself and transmitted by Ibn Ishaq. It is a sirah report rather than an authenticated hadith, and hadith scholars differ over the strength of its chain. According to it, the year after Muhammad's birth was a year of severe drought, and a group of women from Banu Sa'd travelled to Makkah hoping to nurse infants from well-off households.

Among them was a gentle woman named Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb al-Sa'diyyah, accompanied by her husband al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza and their infant nursing son, 'Abdullah. Halimah's family was so impoverished that their elderly she-donkey limped from exhaustion, lagging far behind the caravan, while their solitary she-camel yielded not a single drop of milk, leaving their own baby crying from hunger through sleepless desert nights.
A nomadic encampment amidst the rocky passes and scrub vegetation of the desert.
The Orphan Child and the Hesitation of the Nurses

Upon reaching Makkah, the foster mothers sought out infants of prominent chieftains. The infant Muhammad was presented to several women, but each turned away upon learning that his father 'Abdullah was deceased. The foster mothers reasoned that an orphan's grandfather or widowed mother might offer only modest remuneration compared to an affluent living father who could bestow lavish gifts.

Every woman in the company found a foster child except Halimah, who had arrived last due to her feeble mount. Reluctant to return to her homeland empty-handed to the mockery of her peers, she said to her husband: 'By God, I loathe to return among my companions without a nursling; I shall go to that orphan and take him.' Al-Harith replied with quiet wisdom: 'There is no harm in doing so; perhaps God will place a blessing in him for us.'

'By God, I had no sooner taken him into my bosom than my breasts flowed with milk so abundantly that he drank until he was satisfied, and with him his foster brother drank his fill; then both slept peacefully, whereas before we had not known sleep.' — Halimah al-Sa'diyyah (recorded by Ibn Hisham)
The Manifestation of Divine Blessing (Barakah)

From that very hour, an unmistakable aura of grace enveloped Halimah's household. That night, her husband went to their emaciated she-camel and discovered her udders unexpectedly brimming with rich, sweet milk. Husband and wife drank to their fill and slept in deep, tranquil comfort for the first time in months. In the morning, al-Harith said to his wife: 'Know, O Halimah, by God, you have taken a blessed soul.'

On the return journey across the desert, Halimah mounted her once-feeble donkey, carrying the infant Muhammad in her lap. To the astonishment of her companions, the beast suddenly strode forward with energetic vitality, outpacing the entire company so swiftly that the other riders called out: 'O daughter of Abu Dhu'ayb, woe to you! Wait for us! Is this not the very donkey upon which you set out?' Halimah answered smilingly: 'Yes, by God, it is the same.'

When they arrived in the territory of Banu Sa'd, the barren valley remained parched for others, yet whenever Halimah's small flock of sheep and goats went out to graze, they returned at dusk with swollen udders full of milk, while the flocks of their neighbors returned empty and dry. The other bedouins would instruct their shepherds: 'Graze where the shepherd of the daughter of Abu Dhu'ayb grazes,' yet their animals still returned barren, while Halimah's family thrived in abundance.
Life Among the Shepherds and Desert Eloquence

Halimah is reported to have said that the boy grew in a way unlike other children, so that he was sturdy before his time. He lived alongside his foster brother 'Abdullah and his foster sisters Anisah and Hudhafah (known as al-Shayma', who is reported to have carried him and sung verses to him), and went out with them among the young sheep under the open desert sky.

This upbringing gave him a share of the pure Arabic of the desert. A report in the sirah literature, whose chain is weak, has him say: 'I am the most Arab of you: I am from Quraysh, and I was nursed among Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr.'
The Cleansing of the Heart (Shaqq al-Sadr)

While he was still a small child among Banu Sa'd, an extraordinary event occurred. Sahih Muslim records, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik, that Jibril (Gabriel) came to him while he was playing with the other boys. In Ibn Ishaq's account it took place some months after Halimah had brought him back from a visit to Makkah, when he was about four years old.

In the wording of Sahih Muslim, Jibril took hold of him and threw him down, split open his chest and took out his heart. He extracted a clot from it and said: 'This is the portion of Satan in you.' He then washed the heart in a basin of gold with Zamzam water, closed it, and returned it to its place. The boys ran to his foster mother, saying: 'Muhammad has been killed!' They came to him and found him pale. Anas said: 'I used to see the trace of that stitching on his chest.' Ibn Ishaq's account, attributed to Halimah, speaks instead of two men in white garments and adds further details; it is a separate sirah report.

According to Ibn Ishaq, Halimah and her husband feared for the boy after this event, and she brought him back to Makkah and returned him to his mother Aminah and his grandfather 'Abd al-Muttalib. Most biographers say he was then about four or five years old.
